title: Tamsin and the Parish
premise: Estate lawyer Wren Sterling is summoned to the village of Ashcombe to read the will of Edith Parish, a woman who vanished eleven years ago and was declared dead in absentia. The will is dated three years after her disappearance, and tucked inside it is her diary — which continues past the date she was last seen. As Wren reads, the diary's entries begin describing Wren's own arrival, word for word. To survive, Wren must reopen the case everyone buried: the drowning of Edith's brother, ruled an accident by a parish that closed ranks around its most powerful family. The truth leads to a living Edith, hidden by those who loved her and hunted by the man who tried to kill her, and to a trial where loyalty and justice finally collide.
about_author: Marguerite Thackeray spent a decade as a probate clerk in rural England before turning to fiction, giving her mysteries an insider's knowledge of wills, estates, and the secrets families file away. She writes from a converted tithe barn in Dorset, where she claims every village has one closed case too many.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Wren Sterling arrives in rain-soaked Ashcombe to execute the estate of Edith Parish, dead eleven years — yet the will bears a date three years after her disappearance. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: professional unease curdling into fascination as the solicitor's old files reveal sealed records and a parish eager to be done with it.

chapters.title: Ashcombe's Closed Ranks
chapters.summary: Wren interviews the beneficiaries: Edith's bitter cousin Ruth, the vicar who signed the death petition, and landowner Charles Fenwick, whose family owns half the valley. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: mounting claustrophobia as every villager repeats the same rehearsed grief — and the same warning to leave it alone.

chapters.title: The Diary
chapters.summary: Among Edith's effects Wren finds a diary; its final entry describes Wren reading it, verbatim, dated tomorrow. POV: Wren, with diary excerpts in Edith's voice. Emotional beat: cold dread — someone is watching, or something impossible is happening, and either way Wren cannot put it down.

chapters.title: Three Accidents
chapters.summary: Wren recalls the three deaths she quietly solved before — each ruled accidental, each staged. Comparing methods, she recognizes the same careful hand in Edith's disappearance. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: grim recognition that this killer is patient, local, and still protected by the parish's silence.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Drowned
chapters.summary: Digging into the closed case: Edith's brother Thomas drowned in the mill pond in 2009, ruled misadventure. The diary suggests he found something in the Fenwick accounts. POV: alternating Wren and diary-Edith. Emotional beat: righteous anger as Wren realizes the 'closed' case is the keystone of everything.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession, Almost
chapters.summary: Cousin Ruth, drunk on sherry and guilt, hints Edith didn't drown herself — then recants by morning and begs Wren to stop. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: frustrated tenderness; Ruth is protecting someone, and fear has fossilized into loyalty.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Forensic examination confirms the diary's later pages are genuinely Edith's handwriting — written after her disappearance. Someone kept writing as her, for years. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: vertigo; the mystery shifts from 'what happened' to 'who is still doing this.'

chapters.title: The Vicar's Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren finds the vicar has been receiving anonymous payments routed through church restoration funds — hush money with a conscience. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: disillusionment; even the parish's moral center took the money, and his shame makes him the first crack in the wall.

chapters.title: Someone in the House
chapters.summary: Wren's cottage is searched overnight; the diary is nearly taken, and a page torn from it is left behind like a message. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: violation and defiance — the watcher has escalated from observation to threat, and Wren refuses to run.

chapters.title: What Thomas Found
chapters.summary: Reconstructing Thomas Parish's last weeks: he'd uncovered Fenwick land fraud that would have bankrupted the estate and implicated half the parish's gentry. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: cold clarity — the motive wasn't passion but inheritance, the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: The Trial Date
chapters.summary: A local journalist reveals Fenwick is about to stand trial for fraud after all — the case everyone swore was closed, resurrected by an anonymous evidence packet. The trial begins in ten days. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: urgency; whoever sent the packet wants the past aired before someone silences it again.

chapters.title: Midnight at the Mill
chapters.summary: Following the diary's clues, Wren searches the ruined mill and finds Thomas's hidden ledger — and signs someone was living there until very recently. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: electric hope; Edith may not just be alive, she may be the anonymous sender.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Price
chapters.summary: Ruth finally confesses: she helped Edith disappear after the 'accident,' hiding her for years out of love — and has been forging the diary entries to keep hope alive. POV: Wren and Ruth. Emotional beat: heartbreak; the impossible diary is an act of devotion, but real entries among them are Edith's own.

chapters.title: The Man Who Watched
chapters.summary: Wren identifies the watcher: Fenwick's fixer, Silas Crane, who staged Thomas's drowning and has been hunting Edith for a decade. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: terror sharpening into resolve; the killer knows Wren has the ledger.

chapters.title: Burned Bridge
chapters.summary: Crane burns the mill ruins with the ledger inside; Wren saves only photographed pages, and the vicar, about to testify, dies in a fall the police call accidental — again. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: fury and grief; the pattern repeating in real time makes Wren the next entry.

chapters.title: Edith
chapters.summary: Following Ruth's final secret, Wren finds Edith Parish alive — aged, watchful, living as a lay caretaker two parishes over. POV: Edith, finally. Emotional beat: wary relief meeting weary courage; Edith agrees to testify only if Wren can prove Thomas's murder first.

chapters.title: Reconstructing the Drowning
chapters.summary: Wren rebuilds the night Thomas died using photographs, tide records, and Crane's own habits, finding the flaw only the killer would know. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: quiet triumph hardening into danger — proof exists, but presenting it paints a target on everyone Wren loves.

chapters.title: The Trap at the Pond
chapters.summary: Wren baits Crane with a fake ledger handoff at the mill pond; Crane comes to kill, and Wren — with Ruth recording — draws out his confession. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: white-knuckle climax; the scene nearly turns lethal before police, tipped by the journalist, arrive.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Crane implicates Fenwick before turning on him; the old order collapses as arrests ripple through the parish. But some guilty villagers will never face court, and Wren must decide whether exposure or mercy serves the dead. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: somber reckoning with the cost of truth.

chapters.title: The Trial Begins
chapters.summary: Fenwick's fraud trial opens with Edith alive in the gallery and Wren's evidence admitted; the parish fills the benches to watch its own history read aloud. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: catharsis — the closed case opened at last, the community forced to witness what its silence bought.

chapters.title: Verdicts
chapters.summary: Fenwick is convicted; Crane pleads to manslaughter in Thomas's death; Ruth faces charges for the forged diary and receives leniency Wren argued for. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: bittersweet closure — the law delivers part of the justice, and Wren accepts that no verdict restores what was lost.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Edith gives Wren the diary's true final page, written that morning: an account of standing in the courtroom, seen at last. She asks Wren to keep solving the cases no one else will open. POV: Wren. Emotional beat: quiet renewal — loyalty and truth reconciled, and a new calling accepted as Wren leaves Ashcombe changed.
